p01.why: Braced list elements are evaluated left to right, so a is 0 and b is 1.

p02.why: The function expression pick() is evaluated before the argument arg().

p03.why: The side effect of i++ is complete before the next full expression.

p04.why: The right side of an assignment, with its side effects, finishes before the store, so i is 2 and j is 3.

p05.why: The object expression of a member call is evaluated before the arguments.

p06.why: Two unsequenced reads of a volatile object are undefined, but nothing requires a diagnostic and there is no main.

p07.why: Plain sequential statements in a constexpr function evaluate to 2.

p08.why: The temporary made for the default argument ends with the call statement, so it is gone before the next statement writes 9.

p09.why: Unsequenced writes to adjacent bit-fields in one memory location are undefined, but compilers do not diagnose it and there is no main.

p10.why: An overloaded << keeps the built-in shift order, so first() runs before second().

p11.why: Clang and GCC warn about unsequenced modifications of i under -Wall, and -Werror makes the warning an error.

p12.why: The calls do not interleave, so the results are 0 and 1 in some order, sum is 1 and counter is 2.

p13.why: Arguments are each evaluated completely in some order, so r is 1 or 10 and i is 2.

p14.why: In a[b], a is evaluated before b.

p15.why: An overloaded assignment keeps the built-in order, right operand first.

p16.why: In a.*b, a is evaluated before b.

p17.why: In a compound assignment the right operand is evaluated before the left.

p18.why: The argument order is unspecified, but the program accepts either order.
